ultrafast-001.question: Which correctly describes the mode-locked state of the many longitudinal modes oscillating in a laser cavity?
choices: Even with random phases, light becomes a regular pulse train if there are enough modes, and the pulse duration is set by the round-trip time
The laser is restricted to a single longitudinal mode, and a modulator outside the cavity varies its intensity with the round-trip period to make short pulses
The phases of the equally spaced modes are locked, so they add up into a pulse every round trip, about as short as the inverse of the total bandwidth
ultrafast-001.explanation: When the phases of N longitudinal modes spaced by Δf = c/(2L) are aligned, the fields of all modes add up together at certain times and cancel at others, giving a pulse train with period 1/Δf (the round-trip time). The pulse duration is about 1/(NΔf), the inverse of the total bandwidth of the locked modes. With random phases the intensity just fluctuates irregularly, the same as continuous light on average, and no regular pulse train forms. Varying the intensity of one mode is intensity modulation; its spectrum is narrow, so fs pulses cannot be obtained. In mode locking, the more modes are aligned, the shorter the pulse.

ultrafast-002.question: In passive mode locking with a saturable absorber, why does a short pulse build up on its own?
choices: A saturable absorber absorbs more as the light gets stronger, so peaks are clipped and the pulse widens each round trip until it finally settles at a fixed width
A saturable absorber absorbs less as the light gets stronger, so intense peaks see lower loss, and over repeated round trips a strong, short pulse is selected
An external high-frequency electrical signal varies the loss of the saturable absorber with the same period as the round-trip time
ultrafast-002.explanation: In a saturable absorber, strong light empties the lower level of the absorption so the absorption saturates and the loss drops. If the light intensity in the cavity has a small fluctuation, its peak sees little loss while the wings and weaker parts see large loss, so with each round trip the peak alone grows stronger and narrower in time. Semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAMs) are used, and Ti:sapphire lasers use an extremely fast effective saturable absorber formed by Kerr self-focusing combined with an aperture (Kerr-lens mode locking). Absorption that increases with intensity is the property of an optical limiter. Varying the loss with an external signal is active mode locking; passive mode locking uses no external signal.

ultrafast-003.question: Which is closest to the peak power of the pulses from a mode-locked laser with an average power of 1 W, a repetition rate of 100 MHz and a pulse duration of 100 fs? (Treat the pulse as a rectangle 100 fs wide.)
choices: About 100 kW
About 1 W
About 10 µW
ultrafast-003.explanation: The energy per pulse is the average power divided by the repetition rate, 1 W / (100×10⁶ Hz) = 10 nJ. Concentrated into 100 fs, this gives a peak power of 10×10⁻⁹ J / 100×10⁻¹⁵ s = 1×10⁵ W, about 100 kW. Put another way, the fraction of time the laser is emitting (the duty cycle) is 100 fs × 100 MHz = 10⁻⁵, so the peak is 10⁵ times the average. About 1 W mistakes the average power for the peak, and about 10 µW wrongly multiplies the average power by the duty cycle. For a sech²-shaped pulse a factor of 0.88 applies, giving about 88 kW. This high peak power is why ultrashort pulses are used for nonlinear optics and micromachining.

ultrafast-004.question: A pulse with a center wavelength of 1030 nm and a spectral width (FWHM) of 10 nm is measured to be 600 fs long. Which is closest to the shortest pulse duration obtainable by compensating dispersion without changing the spectrum? (Assume a Gaussian shape with a time-bandwidth product lower limit of ΔνΔt = 0.441; c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s.)
choices: About 160 fs
About 110 fs
About 600 fs
ultrafast-004.explanation: The frequency width is Δν = cΔλ/λ² = 3.0×10⁸ × 10×10⁻⁹ / (1030×10⁻⁹)² ≈ 2.8 THz. The transform-limited duration is 0.441 / (2.8×10¹²) ≈ 1.56×10⁻¹³ s, about 160 fs, and the product with the measured 600 fs, ΔνΔt ≈ 1.7, is about 4 times the lower limit. This shows that the pulse is chirped, with arrival times that differ by frequency, and applying dispersion of the opposite sign can shorten it to about 160 fs. About 110 fs uses the sech² factor of 0.315, which does not match the Gaussian assumption. Keeping about 600 fs assumes that pulse duration is set by spectral width alone; the time-bandwidth product is a lower limit, and equality holds only without chirp.

ultrafast-005.question: Which correctly describes what happens when a short, unchirped (transform-limited) light pulse passes through a glass plate with normal dispersion?
choices: Shorter-wavelength components travel faster, so short wavelengths lead and long ones trail, and the pulse shortens in time with a higher peak
The temporal shape is unchanged, while dispersion generates new frequency components so that only the spectrum broadens
Longer wavelengths travel faster, so they lead and shorter ones trail; the pulse broadens in time while the spectral shape is unchanged
ultrafast-005.explanation: In a medium with normal dispersion (group-velocity dispersion β₂ > 0, group delay dispersion GDD > 0), longer wavelengths have higher group velocity. The arrival times of the frequency components therefore spread, with long wavelengths (low frequencies) at the front and short wavelengths (high frequencies) at the back, giving an up-chirp in which the instantaneous frequency rises with time. An unchirped pulse, with all components in phase, is already in its shortest state, so dispersion broadens it and never shortens it. Dispersion is a linear effect that only changes the phase at each frequency, so the spectral shape is unchanged. Broadening the spectrum without changing the temporal shape is the signature of intensity-dependent self-phase modulation, which should be distinguished from dispersion.

ultrafast-006.question: A transform-limited Gaussian pulse with a duration of 20 fs (FWHM) at a center wavelength of 800 nm passes through 10 mm of fused silica with a group-velocity dispersion of 36 fs²/mm. Which is closest to the duration of the output pulse? (τ_out = τ₀√(1 + (4 ln2 × GDD/τ₀²)²); ignore higher-order dispersion.)
choices: About 20 fs
About 54 fs
About 70 fs
ultrafast-006.explanation: The group delay dispersion is GDD = 36 fs²/mm × 10 mm = 360 fs². Since 4 ln2 × 360 / 20² ≈ 2.50, τ_out = 20 × √(1 + 2.50²) ≈ 20 × 2.69 ≈ 54 fs, broadening by about 2.7 times. About 70 fs computes 20 × (1 + 2.50) without the square root. About 20 fs assumes that just 10 mm of glass has no effect. In the same glass a 100 fs pulse would become about 100.5 fs, almost unchanged, but because the effect scales as GDD/τ₀², shorter pulses broaden sharply. For pulses of a few tens of fs or shorter, even the dispersion of lenses and windows must be compensated.

ultrafast-007.question: Which optical system can be used to compress an up-chirped pulse produced by normal dispersion?
choices: A system that adds plates of the same glass to provide more positive group delay dispersion, so the short wavelengths catch up
A system that cuts out only the center of the spectrum with a narrow bandpass filter, removing the chirped wavelength components at both ends
A system such as a grating pair, prism pair or chirped mirrors giving negative group delay dispersion, so short wavelengths go through first
ultrafast-007.explanation: An up-chirped pulse has long wavelengths at the front and short wavelengths at the back. To compress it, negative GDD is applied to advance the lagging short-wavelength components and delay the long-wavelength ones. Grating pairs and prism pairs create negative GDD because the geometric path length changes with wavelength, and chirped mirrors do so because the depth of reflection in the multilayer changes with wavelength. Adding glass adds dispersion of the same sign, broadening the pulse further. Narrowing the spectrum with a bandpass filter actually lengthens the transform-limited duration because of the time-bandwidth lower limit, so no shorter pulse results.

ultrafast-008.question: In chirped-pulse amplification (CPA), what is the main purpose of stretching the pulse in time before amplification?
choices: To lower the peak power, avoiding nonlinear effects such as self-focusing in the amplifier and optical damage, then compress the pulse back after amplification
Stretching the pulse also broadens its spectrum, which makes full use of the amplifier's wide gain bandwidth out to its edges
A stretched pulse shortens naturally through gain saturation in the amplifier, so short pulses are obtained without a compressor
ultrafast-008.explanation: Amplifying a fs pulse directly would push the peak power to around 10 GW even at an energy of 1 mJ, so Kerr self-focusing and self-phase modulation would distort the waveform and damage the gain medium and mirrors. In CPA a stretcher such as a grating arrangement applies large dispersion to stretch the pulse by 10⁴, for example from 100 fs to 1 ns, lowering the peak power by the same factor before amplification, and finally a compressor with the opposite dispersion restores the original duration. Dispersion does not change the spectral shape, so stretching does not broaden the spectrum. Nor does the pulse shorten on its own in the amplifier; the compressor is essential. CPA made TW-class peak powers possible even with tabletop systems.

ultrafast-009.question: In one method, the spectrum is broadened by self-phase modulation in an optical fiber (or a gas-filled hollow-core fiber) and negative dispersion is then applied, giving a pulse shorter than the input pulse. Why does this method shorten the pulse?
choices: Self-phase modulation itself compresses the pulse in time, and the negative dispersion only undoes the broadening caused by positive dispersion during propagation
The spectrum broadened by self-phase modulation is nearly linearly chirped near the center, so aligning the phases with negative dispersion gives a shorter pulse
Self-phase modulation narrows the spectrum and raises the peak intensity, at which the absorption in the fiber saturates and trims the wings of the pulse
ultrafast-009.explanation: In self-phase modulation the phase changes in proportion to the intensity I(t), so the instantaneous frequency shifts, lower at the front of the pulse and higher at the back. New frequencies are generated and the spectrum broadens, but without dispersion the temporal shape does not change. Near the center the chirp is nearly proportional to time, so applying negative GDD with a prism pair or chirped mirrors brings the components of the broadened spectrum together in time, giving a short pulse close to the transform limit. The time compression happens at the dispersion-compensation stage, not in self-phase modulation itself. It is neither a spectral narrowing effect nor absorption saturation. Near the edges of the spectrum the chirp departs from linear, so a small pedestal remains after compression.

ultrafast-010.question: Which correctly describes measuring the duration of a pulse of about 100 fs by intensity autocorrelation using second-harmonic generation (SHG)?
choices: A photodetector is too slow, but the width of the autocorrelation trace equals the pulse duration directly, so no pulse shape needs to be assumed
Recording the second harmonic versus delay uniquely determines even the asymmetric shape of the pulse front and back and the sign of the chirp
The pulse is split in two with a delay, the second harmonic from their overlap is recorded versus delay, and the width is divided by a shape factor (√2 for a Gaussian)
ultrafast-010.explanation: Even the fastest photodetectors and oscilloscopes respond in a few ps at best, so a 100 fs pulse cannot be measured. Intensity autocorrelation uses the pulse itself as a gate: the delay τ between the two halves of the split pulse is varied while the strength of the second harmonic from a nonlinear crystal, ∫I(t)I(t − τ)dt, is recorded. The autocorrelation is wider than the pulse, by √2 times for a Gaussian and about 1.54 times for a sech² shape, so a shape is assumed for the conversion. For example, an autocorrelation width of 141 fs means about 100 fs for a Gaussian. The autocorrelation is always symmetric, so asymmetry of the pulse and the sign of the chirp cannot be determined; methods that also retrieve the phase, such as FROG, are needed for that.

ultrafast-011.question: An optical frequency comb has a repetition rate f_rep = 250 MHz and a carrier-envelope offset frequency f_ceo = 20 MHz. The beat frequency between a continuous-wave laser of unknown frequency and the comb mode with mode number n = 1.2×10⁶ is 30 MHz, and the laser frequency is known to be above that mode. Which is closest to the laser frequency? (fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo)
ultrafast-011.explanation: Since 1.2×10⁶ × 250 MHz = 300 THz, the mode frequency is fₙ = 300 THz + 20 MHz = 300.000020 THz. The laser is 30 MHz above this mode, so it is at 300.000020 THz + 30 MHz = 300.000050 THz. 300.000030 THz forgets f_ceo, and 299.999990 THz takes the beat on the wrong side. The beat frequency alone cannot tell above from below, so in practice f_rep or another parameter is changed slightly and the sign is found from whether the beat rises or falls, while the mode number n is found from a coarse measurement with a wavemeter. If f_rep and f_ceo are locked to a microwave frequency standard, the optical frequency can be measured with that accuracy.

ultrafast-012.question: Each time a pulse makes one round trip of the cavity, the phase offset between the carrier and the envelope (the carrier-envelope phase) advances by Δφ = π/2. For a repetition rate of 100 MHz, which is closest to the offset frequency f_ceo? (f_ceo = (Δφ/2π) f_rep)
choices: 25 MHz
50 MHz
About 157 MHz
ultrafast-012.explanation: f_ceo = (π/2)/(2π) × 100 MHz = 100 MHz / 4 = 25 MHz. In the cavity, dispersion of the medium makes the phase velocity of the carrier differ from the group velocity of the envelope, so on each round trip the carrier crests slip by Δφ relative to the envelope peak. In the spectrum of the pulse train this slip corresponds to shifting every mode by f_ceo, giving fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo. 50 MHz is the value for Δφ = π. About 157 MHz multiplies by Δφ ≈ 1.57 without dividing by 2π; because Δφ repeats every 2π, f_ceo is normally expressed as a value between 0 and f_rep, so it does not exceed 100 MHz. Δφ changes with temperature and pump power, so f_ceo is measured and controlled.

ultrafast-013.question: When f_ceo is measured by f-2f self-referencing, why must the comb spectrum span at least one octave (a range over which the frequency doubles)?
choices: With a one-octave spectrum the pulse becomes shorter than one optical cycle, so f_ceo is fixed at zero and easier to measure
The beat between the two modes at the ends of the octave becomes twice f_rep, so it can be distinguished from f_rep and read as f_ceo
The second harmonic 2fₙ of a low-side mode fₙ beats with the high-side mode f₂ₙ to give f_ceo, which requires components at both fₙ and 2fₙ
ultrafast-013.explanation: f_ceo is a shift common to all modes, so it cannot be obtained from beats between modes (integer multiples of f_rep). In the f-2f method, components on the low-frequency side of the spectrum are frequency-doubled in a nonlinear crystal and overlapped with modes on the high-frequency side of the original spectrum. Since 2(nf_rep + f_ceo) − (2nf_rep + f_ceo) = f_ceo, the beat gives f_ceo directly. This requires fₙ and 2fₙ to be in the same spectrum, that is, a bandwidth of at least one octave, usually achieved by broadening the spectrum in photonic crystal fiber or similar. Having an octave does not make f_ceo zero. Beats between modes contain no information about f_ceo.

ultrafast-014.question: In an optical frequency comb with a repetition rate f_rep = 250 MHz, f_rep changes by just 1 Hz while f_ceo is held constant. Which is closest to the change in frequency of a mode at about 300 THz (mode number n = 1.2×10⁶)?
choices: About 1.2 MHz
1 Hz
About 1.2 GHz
ultrafast-014.explanation: Since fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo, with f_ceo constant Δfₙ = nΔf_rep = 1.2×10⁶ × 1 Hz = 1.2×10⁶ Hz, about 1.2 MHz. Because the mode number is large, a tiny change in f_rep is magnified, like a lever, in the optical frequency. 1 Hz assumes every mode moves by the same amount, which is what happens when f_ceo changes by 1 Hz. About 1.2 GHz is the value for Δf_rep = 1 kHz, a mix-up of units. The relative change Δf/f is nearly the same, 4×10⁻⁹, for f_rep and for the optical frequency, so determining optical frequencies precisely requires stabilizing f_rep with high accuracy or locking one of the modes to a stable optical reference.

ultrafast-015.question: For which pulses does the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) strongly affect experimental results? (Center wavelength 800 nm; one optical cycle is about 2.7 fs.)
choices: Long pulses with a FWHM of about 1 ns. The more oscillations within the envelope, the more the CEP slips accumulate and matter
Pulses with a FWHM of about 5 fs, whose envelope holds only about two optical cycles. The peak field strength changes with the CEP
It is the same regardless of pulse duration; the CEP sets the pulse energy and intensity envelope shape, so it matters for every pulse
ultrafast-015.explanation: One cycle of 800 nm light is λ/c ≈ 2.7 fs, so the FWHM of a 5 fs pulse contains only about 1.9 cycles. With a CEP of 0 the carrier crest coincides with the envelope peak and the maximum field is large, while at π/2 the crest is offset and the maximum drops. Tunnel ionization, high-harmonic generation and attosecond pulse generation, which depend on the instantaneous field, are sensitive to this difference. A 100 fs pulse holds about 37 cycles, so changing the CEP hardly changes the maximum field, and for ns pulses it is completely negligible. The CEP is the phase of the carrier and does not change the pulse energy or the intensity envelope.
